title: Knowledge-guided machine learning for disentangling Pacific sea surface temperature variability across timescales
abstract: Abstract Global weather and climate patterns are strongly influenced by dominant modes of anomalous Pacific sea surface temperature (SST) variability, including the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), Pacific Meridional Mode (PMM), and Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO). However, disentangling these modes of variability remains challenging due to their spatial overlap and nonlinear coupling, which violate the assumptions of traditional linear methods. We develop a Knowledge-Guided AutoEncoder (KGAE) that uses spatiotemporal constraints and a gradient-based sparsity incentive to identify physically interpretable modes of detrended SST variability, each defined by a single broad characteristic timescale, without the need for predefined temporal filters or thresholds. The KGAE separates ENSO-like modes on 2- and 3–7-year timescales, as well as a decadal mode with characteristics reminiscent of the PDO and PMM, each with distinct spatial patterns. We perturb each latent dimension and use finite differences to characterize the state-independent and state-dependent sensitivities. title: Progress toward forecasting excessive rainfall with random forests based on a deterministic convection-allowing model
abstract: Abstract Machine learning applied to high-resolution numerical weather prediction forecasts is gaining popularity for prediction of high-impact weather events, but questions remain on how to design such systems. Building off prior work, we describe sensitivity experiments using a random forest (RF) system for excessive rainfall prediction using the deterministic High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR). We find that applying an RF trained on HRRRv3 to daily forecasts from HRRRv4 does not significantly degrade results. In terms of the spatial aggregation of predictor information for the RF, we find that forecasts are significantly improved when the system uses data from all nearby model gridpoints, rather than just sparse input points, particularly for events featuring small-scale precipitation maxima. Forecasts are also improved when predictors are averaged across multiple HRRR initializations rather than taken from a single HRRR initialization, as the RF is better able to learn relationships with the reduced uncertainty of the time-lagged ensemble mean predictors. title: Dune Crestline Mapping With Deep Learning Reveals Large‐Scale Dune Patterns in NW China
abstract: Abstract Dune crestlines encode sediment transport dynamics and atmospheric forcing, yet their large‐scale quantification has been constrained by labor‐intensive mapping or limited resolution. Here we develop an attention‐augmented U‐Net model to automatically extract crestlines from ∼1 m resolution satellite imagery. Trained on 17,798 manually annotated crestlines, the model maps over 4 million crest features across the Badain Jaran and Tengger Deserts, yielding an unprecedented high‐resolution data set of dune‐field organization. Integrating ERA5‐Land wind reanalysis and Copernicus digital elevation model‐derived equivalent sand thickness, we quantify spatial variations in crest orientation, spacing, sinuosity, and hierarchy with respect to boundary conditions. Crest orientations largely agree with predictions from the bed‐instability mode under sand‐covered conditions, while deviations near upwind margins and transport corridors indicate elongation‐mode preference under sand‐starved bed. title: Batched NN 4D-Var: a performant hybrid model framework for the Integrated Forecasting System
abstract: Hybrid forecasting systems combining machine learning and numerical weather prediction offer a promising route toward improved forecast skill while preserving physical consistency. In this study, we investigate online learning of state-dependent model-error corrections within the Integrated Forecasting System using 4D-Var. Building on previous work, we represent model error using a neural network embedded within the forecast model and trained from observations through the data assimilation cycle. First, we introduce a targeted variant of neural-network 4D-Var in which only the neural-network parameters are estimated, while the atmospheric state is provided by a precomputed analysis. We then propose a batched extension that processes assimilation windows in random order and averages parameter increments over multiple windows, drawing inspiration from mini-batch stochastic optimization. Experiments are conducted with the Integrated Forecasting System of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts at an intermediate resolution. title: Continuous mapping of deep convective cores from geostationary infrared imagery using a multi-scale composite-loss conditional GAN trained on GPM-DPR
abstract: Abstract Tropical convection is characterized by vertical motions over short spatial and temporal scales, producing wide convective systems associated with intense precipitation and severe weather. Geostationary satellites provide continuous observations of cloud-top properties, but linking them to the internal dynamical structure of convective cores remains challenging. This work introduces a generative deep-learning framework that produces geostationary-like, continuous monitoring of a radar-derived proxy of the underlying structures’ vertical extent: the Echo-Top Height at 20 dBZ (ETH20). Deep convective cores are identified by the echo tops reaching a high-altitude level (> 10 km). Collocated Meteosat second generation SEVIRI infrared imagery and GPM radar observations over tropical Atlantic and Africa are used to train the retrieval of ETH20 from multispectral infrared sequences. The proposed method is a conditional generative adversarial network (CGAN) physically constrained by a composite multi-scale loss. title: NNJA—a curated archive of Earth system observations from 1970s to present for reanalysis and data-driven model development
abstract: Abstract The NOAA-NASA Joint Archive (NNJA pronounced like the word ninja) is a publicly accessible, curated collection of Earth system observations spanning 1979 to present, created to accelerate reanalysis production, support development of artificial intelligence (AI) applications, and enable access to the observational record underlying modern reanalyses. The archive encompasses atmospheric satellite radiances and conventional measurements, in-situ ocean profiles, sea ice concentrations and freeboard retrievals, and land surface observations from over 60 sensors provided by NOAA, NASA, and their partners. The number of atmospheric records increases from around 10 6 observations per day in 1979 to around 10 8 in the modern era. The dataset extends into near-real time through continuous archival of the NOAA operational data. NNJA observations are distributed through Amazon Web Services in formats compatible with established data assimilation systems and are accompanied by channel-level black and white lists that capture the quality history of the satellite record. title: Future Changes in Early-Season Severe Weather: A Comparison of Machine Learning and Convection-Permitting Dynamical Downscaling
abstract: Abstract Hazardous convective weather (HCW; i.e. tornadoes, large hail, and severe wind) is a damaging phenomenon caused by thunderstorms. However, future spatiotemporal changes in HCW are unknown, in part associated with the high computational cost of convection-permitting (≤ 4 km) global climate model simulations. We used the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model to conduct convection-permitting simulations to project future changes in early-season (January–April) HCW over the central-to-eastern U.S. Simulations were performed for a historical period (1991–2000) and a future period (2091–2100) forced by Representative Concentration Pathway 8.5. HCW occurrence, defined as updraft vertical velocity (UVV) exceeding 18 m s −1 in a favorable environment, is projected to increase by 173% in the future based on convection-permitting simulations, with a 62% increase in the frequency of days with HCW. Future increases in HCW are supported by increases in UVV, HCW environmental favorability driven by CAPE, and the conditional probability of HCW occurrence. title: Investigating the Use of Geostationary Satellites to Identify Thunderstorm Initiation with the LightningCast and ThunderCast Machine Learning Models
abstract: Abstract Satellite spectral bands have been used to identify patterns associated with thunderstorms such as strong updrafts, deep vertical development, cloud-top cooling, and cloud particle phase. Because of this, satellite data are incorporated into forecasting applications for identification of initiating thunderstorms including the Day Cloud Phase Distinction (DCPD) and Nighttime Microphysics (NtMicro) false color red-green-blue (RGB) composite imagery and machine learning models for short-term forecasting (nowcasting) of thunderstorms and their hazards. However, initiating lightning-producing and non-lightning-producing convective storms can appear similar in satellite imagery, making it difficult to determine which developing storms will become mature thunderstorms. As a consequence, nowcasting models relying solely on satellite imagery, such as LightningCast and ThunderCast, can be imprecise when used to nowcast at local scales. To further verify this and examine the conditions under which non-lightning-producing convective storms appear similar to developing thunderstorms in satellite imagery, four case studies are presented with LightningCast’s and ThunderCast’s predictions

title: Data‐driven emulation of flow‐dependent background‐error variance in variational data assimilation
abstract: Abstract Accurate representation of flow‐dependent background‐error covariance is essential for modern ensemble–variational data assimilation systems, but estimating ensemble covariance from sufficiently large ensembles remains computationally expensive. In this work, we propose a machine‐learning approach to emulate ensemble‐derived background‐error variance fields from severely undersampled ensembles. Machine‐learning models are trained to map variance estimates derived from five‐member ensembles to those obtained from operational 50‐member European Centre for Medium‐Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble of data assimilations (EDA). The trained models are deployed within a hybrid ensemble four‐dimensional variational data assimilation system and evaluated over an independent three‐month period in an operational numerical weather prediction environment. In these experiments, the full ensemble is retained for the non‐variance components of the background‐error covariance, so the study tests machine‐learning emulation of the variance component rather than finding a complete low‐cost replacement for the operational ensemble system. title: Data-driven and physics-guided hindcasting of measured wave spectra
abstract: Short-range hindcasts of measured wave spectra are evaluated using a recurrent model initialized by one hourly buoy spectrum and supplied with local wind, fetch and depth. Measurements from three Baltic Sea stations are combined for training in 2017--2020, validation in 2021 and testing in 2022. ERA5 reanalysis supplies winds throughout the twelve-hour prediction interval. The comparison examines supervision of spectral variance, peak frequency and peak amplitude, followed by empirical wind-sea bounds and a local relaxation constraint. Variance and peak-frequency supervision gives the lowest spectral error within the data-driven comparison, whereas additional peak-amplitude supervision gives the lowest wave-height error. In the matched physical comparison, relaxation reduces height RMSE by 5.01\% to \PhPtwoHs{}~cm. Extending this constraint through hours 13--24, without spectral targets at those hours, reduces primary spectral RMSE by 2.31\% to \PhPthreeSpec{}~$\unitE$. Upper-bound constraints increase errors. title: Probabilistic Machine Learning for Short-Term Atmospheric Seeing Forecasting
abstract: Accurate short-term forecasting of atmospheric seeing is of significant interest for astronomical observations and free-space optical communication systems, where rapid variations in optical turbulence can affect system performance and operational planning. In this work, we benchmark machine learning models for predicting atmospheric seeing up to two hours in advance, with a particular focus on probabilistic forecasting and uncertainty quantification. We compare two probabilistic approaches, Gaussian Processes (GPs) and a normalizing-flow- based model (FloTS), against deterministic recurrent neural network (RNN) and long short-term memory (LSTM) baselines. All models are trained and evaluated on seeing measurements from the Maunakea summit. We assess the models using both deterministic metrics, including the root mean square error and the Pearson correlation coefficient, and probabilistic metrics that evaluate the quality and calibration of predictive uncertainty estimates. The results show that deep learning approaches outperform standard recurrent networks for short-term forecasting, with LSTM and FloTS achieving the best overall predictive accuracy. title: FogTTA: Online Test-Time Adaptation for Robust Transformer-based Object Detection in Foggy Weather
abstract: Object detection models for autonomous driving commonly experience substantial performance drops when deployed under adverse weather due to the domain shift between training data and real-world operating conditions. This degradation is especially evident when models trained on clear-weather images encounter foggy environments with reduced visibility and contrast. To address this challenge, we introduce FogTTA, an online test-time adaptation framework designed to improve the robustness of Transformer-based object detectors in fog. Using RF-DETR as the underlying object detector, FogTTA enables real-time adaptation to the streaming target domain without requiring source data or retraining. The framework follows a teacher-student design, where the deployed model serves as the teacher and generates pseudo labels from weakly augmented target inputs. These predictions are subsequently refined through non-maximum suppression and confidence filtering. The student model then learns from strongly augmented target sample using the Varifocal loss to mitigate pseudo-label noise. title: YingLan: A Multimodal Ocean Foundation Model for Unified Representation Learning from Heterogeneous Observations
abstract: Multimodal ocean modeling remains challenging due to substantial heterogeneity in data structures, physical semantics, and spatiotemporal characteristics across satellite imagery, gridded oceanographic fields, and buoy observations. Existing approaches largely focus on task-specific ocean modeling, while learning transferable representations from heterogeneous observations remains an open problem. To address this challenge, we propose YingLan, a multimodal ocean foundation model that integrates physics-attribute-conditioned dynamic encoding, Spatiotemporal Increment Coupling (STIC), and ocean-state evolution-aware pretraining. Specifically, the dynamic encoding mechanism generates adaptive input projections conditioned on physical semantics and observation characteristics, enabling flexible representation of heterogeneous ocean variables. STIC models multiscale spatiotemporal dependencies through cross-scale interactions of latent temporal increments. The pretraining strategy further combines masked observation reconstruction with temporal evolution objectives to facilitate the learning of coherent ocean-state representations across different prediction horizons. title: Data-driven identification of atmospheric factors controlling a meso-convective system using 1000-member ensemble simulations
abstract: Abstract Most studies on meso-convective systems have identified favorable atmospheric conditions through subjective analysis of deterministic outputs or selected ensemble members. In contrast, this study applies three objective data analysis methods to 1000-member ensemble simulations of the July 2020 Kyushu heavy rainfall event: ensemble sensitivity analysis (ESA), partial least squares (PLS), and, for the first time in ensemble-based sensitivity analysis, generative topographic maps (GTM), a nonlinear machine-learning method. The large ensemble size permits these analyses without localization, preserving physically meaningful remote correlations. All three methods converge on a consistent mechanism: heavy rainfall is most sensitive to a deepened Baiu frontal depression west of Kyushu with enhanced low-level moisture flux from the west rather than the southwest. The GTM analysis adds what the linear methods cannot provide: the full range of scenarios present in the ensemble, and the critical differences between the favorable and the unfavorable configurations. title: Tropical Cyclone Attributes in Sparse Autoencoder Features of an AI Weather Model
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) weather models now forecast weather events skillfully, but how they represent these events internally remains unknown. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide sparse features for probing hidden states, but how information about multiple physical attributes of an event is organized across them remains unclear. Using tropical cyclones in GraphCast as a test case, we analyze 2,115 six-hourly timesteps from 205 cyclones, relating SAE activations to position, intensity, and pressure structure across five Layer-8 decompositions and 16 processor layers. Each attribute relates to multiple features; position and pressure-structure relations overlap in a smaller subset. This organization recurs across independent SAEs and layers without feature alignment. In deeper layers, the leading position feature aligns better with position and pressure structure six hours ahead than at present. These results suggest that the organization of physical-attribute relations provides a reproducible level of description for interpreting cyclone-related information in GraphCast.

title: Disentangling forced and internal components in observed climate evolution using spatiotemporal deep learning
abstract: Attribution of observed historical climate evolution to externally forced change and internal variability is fundamental to understanding climate change and evaluating climate models. Yet such attribution remains challenging because the forced response is intertwined with internal variability in observations. Here, we develop a convolutional long short-term memory network (ConvLSTM) to disentangle these two components. Trained and evaluated using large-ensemble simulations from multiple climate models, ConvLSTM consistently outperforms existing model-based, statistical, and machine-learning approaches. Applying ConvLSTM to observations reveals an evolving spatial pattern of the forced response and substantial contributions from internal variability to recent multidecadal climate trends. title: TerraNostra-Bench: Benchmarking Spatial Downscaling and Temporal Rollout for Global 1-km Land-Use Reconstruction
abstract: Uncertainty in the terrestrial carbon cycle remains a major constraint in climate projections, partly due to imperfect land surface representations in Earth system models. We propose a data-driven framework for high-resolution land-use reconstruction, treated as a semantic-segmentation task, that combines coarse-resolution scenario data and climate classification with static geophysical features to produce annual land-use maps at 1 km resolution. We introduce TerraNostra-Bench, a change-aware evaluation protocol that separates spatial downscaling from autoregressive temporal rollout and scores models on the rare land-use-change pixels rather than the dominant static background. Using it, we compare convolutional (U-Net) and transformer (Swin) backbones in autoregressive and non-autoregressive schemes against persistence, linear, and shallow convolutional baselines. The autoregressive prior is the most informative input yet accumulates error over long rollouts: autoregressive models lose 5.7-7.2 accuracy points over 13 years, against 2.2-2.8 for non-autoregressive models. title: From Weather to Enhanced Weathering: Weather Foundation Models for Carbon Dioxide Removal at Operational Scale
abstract: Enhanced Rock Weathering (ERW) is a carbon removal solution with the potential to remove gigatons of CO$_2$ per year, but quantifying that removal today requires dense soil sampling and laboratory analysis. We evaluate five weather Foundation Models (FMs) as frozen encoders feeding lightweight decoders, under a leave-one-field-out protocol on 5,192 chronosequences from 264 fields across Brazil and the US. To our knowledge, this is the first holistic evaluation of weather FMs for ERW and the largest evaluation on operational ERW data. We find that across weather FMs, representations transfer to ERW: our best model, TerraNova-ERW, built on Aurora 1.5, positively orders measurements within fields it has never seen. Zero-shot prediction of a new field's mean removal is not yet feasible, and we attribute this to data scale: the same architecture excels on $\sim$$10^5$ natural-weathering sequences, anchoring the scale we expect ERW data must reach. title: Observation Assimilation Transformer: Probabilistic Weather Analysis from Sparse Station Observations
abstract: We present the Observation Assimilation Transformer (OAT), a geometry-aware neural process that corrects and refines a prior numerical weather prediction (NWP) field into a high-resolution posterior field by assimilating sparse observations. OAT is an encoder-decoder transformer that considers a set of observed locations and their NWP prior to condition predictions at a set of arbitrary unobserved query locations. Its sparse attention mechanism makes it scalable to thousands of station observations and depends on relative positions between locations, never on the absolute coordinates. The model allows for partially missing observations, predictions at arbitrary continuous locations without grid projection, and outputs are parametric distributions. A station-randomized training algorithm is developed with continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) loss. We test OAT on two datasets - one at regional scale with hundreds of stations, and one at continental scale with thousands of stations. On these datasets OAT outperforms several baselines and shows well calibrated predictions. title: Foundation-Style Pretraining for Scalable and Transferable Distributed PV Forecasting
abstract: The rapid growth of distributed photovoltaic (PV) generation is increasing the demand for accurate forecasting across large numbers of geographically dispersed stations. Existing approaches are commonly developed for individual sites or specific forecasting horizons, requiring repeated training and maintenance as new stations are integrated and limiting direct reuse at previously unseen sites. To address this scalability gap, this paper presents a domain-specific foundation-style pretraining framework that learns a shared forecasting model from heterogeneous multi-site and multi-horizon PV data. NWP-assisted forecasting is formulated as a sequence-completion problem that unifies historical PV power, meteorological observations, future numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts, and time encodings. Three pretraining objectives are designed and systematically evaluated, including forecast-aligned reconstruction, generic reconstruction, and mixed reconstruction. title: Wet-Biased Data Pipelines Mislead the Training and Evaluation of Generative Precipitation Nowcasting
abstract: Generative models for precipitation nowcasting are trained and evaluated predominantly on wet-biased datasets, which over-represent precipitation events to emphasize rare extremes. Selecting test cases based on target observations is known to favor forecasts that match the selected distribution rather than the intended deployment distribution. We show analytically how this target-dependent sampling also shifts the conditional distribution learned by generative models. When training and test sampling match, even an ideal model learns precisely the distribution favored by evaluation, allowing the evaluation bias to conceal the training bias. Using a fixed satellite-to-radar diffusion model, we demonstrate that target-dependent test sampling can reverse the calibration assessment. The model appears under-predictive on a wet-biased test set but over-predictive on a deployment-representative test set. This result is replicated outside the model's training domain after a seven-year gap. Utilizing classifier-free guidance as an example, we demonstrate how the contradictory calibration assessment can misdirect downstream model development.

title: Spatio-temporal precipitation downscaling at hourly resolution based on km-scale regional simulations
abstract: Effectively preparing for changes in extreme flooding requires understanding present and future rainfall extremes with return periods up to $\sim$100-1000 years, including changes in intensity, spatial structure at km-scale and sub-daily temporal variability. Conventional km-scale climate models give greatly increased realism compared to typical global climate models (GCMs) but are too computationally costly to allow enough simulations for robustly quantifying changes in extremes. This work presents an approach based on video diffusion to generate realistic precipitation at 8.8km-hourly resolution by spatially and temporally downscaling daily, GCM-scale atmospheric variables. The emulator is trained to produce similar output to a $4\times$-coarsening of the Met Office's 2.2km-resolution UK convection-permitting model. An application for such an emulator is to downscale large-ensemble GCM simulations to allow quantification of $\sim$100-1000-year return level rainfall, which in turn can be used to drive hydrological and flood models for improved projections of future changes in flood risk.

title: AirMPA: A Meteorology-to-Pollution Adapter for Global Air Quality Forecasting
abstract: Accurate real-time forecasting of atmospheric pollutants is essential for reducing exposure risks and improving public health. Traditional numerical forecasting systems suffer from incomplete parameterizations, uncertain inputs, and high computational cost. Existing deep learning approaches improve efficiency, but often entangle meteorological and pollutant variables within unified forecasting frameworks, limiting flexibility and pollutant-specific representation learning. To address these challenges, we propose AirMPA, a decoupled autoregressive framework for meteorology-to-pollution forecasting. AirMPA predicts 13 atmospheric pollutants at 0.4° spatial resolution and 12-h temporal resolution using meteorological fields, emission priors, and historical pollutant concentrations. The model is built on an improved Swin-Transformer architecture with zonal release attention and dual-branch fusion, enabling more effective modeling of global transport continuity and heterogeneous pollutant dynamics. title: OceanTensorCube and ST-MMT: A Multimodal Data and Transformer System for Seven-Day Forecasting of Pyropia Bleaching
abstract: Bleaching of cultured Pyropia (laver) causes losses in Korean seaweed farming. We present a system that forecasts bleaching seven days ahead for farm clusters. OceanTensorCube aligns 32 channels from public marine, meteorological, ocean-model and satellite sources on a 30 m grid, and ST-MMT, a 9.2-million-parameter spatiotemporal transformer with hub-style multi-head cross-attention between variable groups, maps a 14-day input window to a seven-day-ahead bleaching probability. On the validation set, a six-seed ensemble detects every reported positive at a false-alarm rate of at most 3.5%, an upper bound because the report-based labels are positive-unlabeled. A same-date control on separately trained models indicates that the architecture discriminates between clusters when the calendar is held fixed. We also report the system's weaknesses: skill falls steeply as the quarterly nutrient survey ages (ROC-AUC 0.94 at 30 days, 0.53 at 129 days), and a single LSTM on cluster-average series outperforms a single ST-MMT, with only the ensemble leading at the operating point. title: Global probabilistic forecasting of air pollution
abstract: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) refers to particulate matter with an aerodynamic diameter of 2.5 micrometre or less. It comes from human activities, such as traffic and industry, and from wildfires, desert dust and gases emitted by vegetation. Short-term exposure to it accounts for about a million deaths a year. Operational forecasts run on grids tens of kilometres wide, which hide the pollution breathed by nearly two hundred million people a day. Machine learning has transformed weather forecasting, but data-driven forecasts of air pollution still blur extremes and lose skill as the air travels. Here we introduce Foehn, a generative model that learns from global kilometre-scale estimates of PM2.5 and computes where the air comes from. Over a year of retrospective forecasts, it outperforms the operational forecast at three stations in four and forecasts at the scale of this hidden exposure. Its ensembles are calibrated, and their mean detects local pollution extremes four days ahead as well as the operational forecast does one day ahead. Such forecasts could warn the millions whom coarse maps miss, once kilometre-scale data are available in real time.

title: Zephyrus-R1: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Weather Reporting
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key method for training AI models in scientific applications, but RL remains difficult when outputs cannot easily be verified against a known ground-truth answer. Natural-language weather forecast reports are one such domain: they translate atmospheric data into assessments of weather evolution, hazards, and uncertainty for both the general public and key decision-makers. Unlike numerical weather-analysis questions, they admit many valid outputs, which limits deterministic verification. To address this, we develop Zephyrus-R1, a practical framework for RL on scientific weather forecast reporting. We focus on three key components of the agentic RL pipeline: reward design, curriculum learning, and an analysis of human-expert alignment. To encourage both report legibility and factual accuracy, we design a reward function that combines a meteorological rubric with bidirectional claim entailment, both evaluated against National Weather Service reference reports. Our framework optimizes this reward in a simulated tool-calling environment, enabling vision-language agents to gather and analyze forecast evidence across regions and lead times befo

title: Beyond the record: evaluating probabilistic AI weather forecasts deep in the tail
abstract: Can probabilistic artificial intelligence (AI) weather forecasts retain skill beyond their training domain? We compare four state-of-the-art AI models (ArchesWeatherGen, U-Cast, WeatherNext2 and GenCast-mini) with the physics-based IFS-ENS over land in 2022, at 1.5° resolution and lead times of 2--10 days. Monthly ERA5 records from 1979--2021 define common historical boundaries, and we characterize new records set in 2022 by their depth, i.e., the exceedance margin relative to local historical variability. Two proper scores, record-threshold weighted CRPS and Brier score, assess the magnitude and probability of record exceedances across all eligible cases, retaining both missed extremes and false alarms. Verified against ERA5, AI models outperform IFS-ENS for heat and cold records at almost every lead and depth. For heat, the advantage strengthens with depth, partly because IFS-ENS over-forecasts deep records, and largely persists for deeper records under HRES-fc0 verification. For wind, gains erode for deeper records and longer leads. Better tail scores can nevertheless coexist with aggregate probability deficits or surpluses, and some improvements arise chiefly on non-exceedances

title: Data-driven forecasting of tropical cloud forest phenology: A dynamical systems and machine learning hybrid approach
abstract: Forecasting how species and ecosystems respond to climate change is a critical challenge in ecology, particularly in hyper-diverse tropical biomes. While traditional phenological models often rely on preconceived functional forms, this study introduces a data-driven hybrid approach that integrates dynamical systems theory with machine learning to forecast flowering and fruiting cycles. Using a robust 35-year dataset from a Venezuelan tropical cloud forest, we reconstruct the system's state-space using delay vectors inspired by Takens' theorem, incorporating climate forcing variables such as temperature and precipitation. The model was trained using Gaussian Process Regression, providing both point predictors and explicit uncertainty estimates. Our results clearly suggest that the synergy between dynamical systems and machine learning effectively captures the non-linear complexities of ecological time series. Specifically, the model achieved higher predictive accuracy for flowering and fruiting. This hybrid framework offers a scalable tool for anticipating phenological mismatches and informing conservation strategies in the face of global environmental change.

title: UtoMe: Observation-Uncertainty-Guided Token Merging for Weather Foundation Models
abstract: Weather transformers process dense reanalysis fields whose reliability varies across variables, locations, and weather regimes. Token merging can reduce computation, but feature similarity alone does not account for this heterogeneous input uncertainty. We introduce UtoMe, an observation-uncertainty-guided token merging framework that combines dynamics saliency with ensemble data assimilation spread as a relative input-reliability proxy. The resulting importance score protects selected tokens as anchors and calibrates bipartite matching between the remaining tokens. Three variants use external uncertainty at both training and inference, during training only, or neither stage. In ERA5 72-hour forecasting at two spatial resolutions, UtoMe improves Overall error over train-time ToMe at matched token budgets. At $1.40625^\circ$ and 50% token reduction, UtoMe-E lowers Overall error from 67.32 to 53.00 at the same 0.55x encoder FLOPs. Small reductions remain close to the full-token baseline; larger reductions incur measurable accuracy losses. title: Spherical Physics-informed Neural Operator with Multi-scale Coupling for Meteorological Downscaling
abstract: Meteorological downscaling is crucial for high-resolution regional climate forecasting and disaster early warning. While neural operators have emerged as a promising paradigm for modeling complex spatiotemporal mappings, existing frameworks often struggle with spherical manifold geometric distortions, inherent atmospheric multi-scale coupling mismatches, and lack of explicit atmospheric laws. We propose the Spherical Physics-informed Neural Operator, which utilizes a Spherical Laplacian Decomposition to partition atmospheric fields into hierarchical frequency components, maintaining exact point-wise correspondence across scales. To evaluate these representations at arbitrary locations, we introduce a localized spherical integral operator that approximates continuous kernel transforms via geometry-aware attention. Dynamical consistency is further enforced by embedding differentiable constraints into the learning process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework attains superior accuracy and zero-shot generalization across various meteorological variables and unseen queries, representing a robust and interpretable solution for global-to-regional meteorological downscaling

title: UDL-RT: A unified differentiable all-sky microwave radiative transfer model with learnable parameterizations
abstract: Radiance-based retrievals and data assimilation require radiative transfer models (RTMs) to simulate radiances and quantify their sensitivities to atmospheric and surface conditions. Conventional RTMs often rely on separately maintained forward, tangent-linear, and adjoint codes, complicating model development and extension. Here, we present the Unified Differentiable and Learnable Radiative Transfer model (UDL-RT), a PyTorch-based framework for all-sky microwave radiative transfer that couples neural-network (NN) parameterizations of gaseous absorption, hydrometeor bulk scattering properties (BSPs), and ocean surface emissivity with an explicit radiative transfer solver in a unified differentiable computational graph. Automatic differentiation directly computes Jacobians with respect to input variables, reducing the model maintenance burden. The NN parameterizations offer flexible representations of complex nonlinear relationships. For example, the NN gas-absorption parameterization reduces the standard deviation of brightness-temperature (TB) errors by approximately 60-85% in the water-vapour channels compared with linear regression. title: Interpretable Machine Learning Reveals Global Nonlinear Responses of Soil Respiration to Climate
abstract: Abstract Soil respiration ( R s ) is a major component of the global carbon cycle, yet its responses to environmental drivers remain poorly constrained. Using 8,111 observations and a SHAP‐interpreted Random Forest model, we identified global response patterns for key environmental drivers of R s . Temperature contributions showed a peaked association with a descriptive maximum of 27.7°C, precipitation contributions plateaued at high values, and leaf area index contributions increased approximately linearly. These results provide a global, data‐driven characterization of peaked temperature and saturating precipitation associations, including how their shapes and supported ranges vary among climate zones. Our results indicate that monotonic assumptions in Earth system models may overlook important nonlinearities and potentially bias estimates of terrestrial carbon flux responses to seasonal climate extremes. Interpretable machine learning therefore provides a transparent framework for evaluating and improving the representation of soil carbon dynamics under climate change.

title: Interpretability of AI weather models via intermediate decoding
abstract: AI weather prediction models are often regarded as black boxes. Despite their impressive skill, there is little understanding of how the input data is processed during inference to produce the forecast. This limitation arises from the use of high-dimensional latent representations in which individual dimensions are no longer directly interpretable in physical terms. To gain insight into how forecasts are constructed, we propose the method of intermediate decoding for AI weather models and apply it to GraphCast, Aurora and ArchesWeather. In this approach, latent states from intermediate depths are decoded back into meteorological fields. To do this, we use the decoder that has been trained to output the forecast at the end of processing. Since latent states at different depths do not share a consistent basis, we train affine transformations that align intermediate latent states with the decoder's expected input space. Applying this framework to the three models yields the following results. First, the skill of forecasts at intermediate stages of processing improves gradually through the processor layers. Second, bypassing all processor blocks shows that the encoder-decoder pair is n

title: Assessing the ability of a stretched‐grid deep‐learning weather prediction model to capture physical balances
abstract: Abstract Weather forecasting has traditionally relied on numerical weather prediction (NWP) models, which simulate weather by solving the governing fluid equations. Recently, the emergence of deep learning weather prediction (DLWP) models has opened a new era in weather forecasting, offering a data‐driven alternative to classical NWP approaches. Regional DLWP models, such as the stretched‐grid model Bris developed by Met Norway, have demonstrated performance on par with or even slightly better than regional NWP models across a range of standard forecast metrics. By overcoming the coarse horizontal resolution that constrained earlier global data‐driven models, the operational use of regional DLWP systems now appears increasingly promising. Nevertheless, the performance of such models during extreme events is generally inferior to that of regional NWP models, and comprehensive evaluations of their ability to generate physically realistic forecasts are still lacking. Here, we present a study comparing the physical consistency of the deterministic version of Bris with the control run of the operational MetCoOp Ensemble Prediction System (MEPS) in forecasting the severe extratropical cy

title: Atmospheric Chemistry-Climate Modeling with an AI Foundation Model
abstract: Atmospheric composition and chemistry-climate interactions are central to predicting future climate change. Yet simulating chemical and aerosol processes is typically the most expensive component of an atmospheric model and is often highly simplified or prescribed entirely. AI weather forecasting foundation models have shown skill rivalling process-based models and are increasingly fine-tuned for new atmospheric tasks. Here, we present the first foundation model to capture interactions between emissions, atmospheric composition, and radiation. We fine-tune the Aurora Earth system foundation model on simulations from the chemistry-climate model UKCA. Our model reproduces daily meteorology, composition, aerosol, and radiation fields of the coupled system with 23 of 27 predicted fields achieving $R^2$ above 0.85 in both the troposphere and stratosphere. It reproduces ozone, CO, and temperature with annual mean biases below 4% and the downwelling shortwave and longwave fluxes to within 6%. Our model remains stable in autoregressive simulation over 50 years while running ~$100\times$ faster than UKCA. title: Can AI Forecast the Extremes? Evaluating Probabilistic Weather Models on Tropical Cyclones
abstract: Weather prediction is undergoing an important shift, with data-driven AI models outperforming leading numerical weather prediction systems on average at a fraction of the computational cost. Yet, whether this success extends to extreme events remains contested. Earlier evaluations have exposed important shortcomings, but have largely focused on deterministic models and metrics, leaving the capabilities of the latest probabilistic models less understood. We conduct an extensive benchmark of tropical cyclone forecasting, comparing GenCast, FourCastNet 3, and FGN with ECMWF's operational physics-based ensemble, IFS-ENS. We develop a suite of probabilistic metrics and diagnostic analyses to assess cyclone tracking, intensity biases, uncertainty, and the wind-pressure relationship that characterizes storm structure. We find that, despite remaining limitations in intensity and ensemble spread, leading AI models substantially outperform IFS-ENS in cyclone tracking: FGN achieves better probabilistic location scores for 90% of evaluated storms in 2025. Further analyses reveal model-specific failure modes and suggest a lingering influence of pretraining data, pointing to opportunities for ta

title: Energy Flow Shapes the Decomposition Dynamics of a Reactive Atmospheric Intermediate
abstract: The unimolecular dynamics of Criegee intermediates depend strongly on their internal energy, which can differ substantially between nascent atmospheric species and laboratory-prepared reactants. Here, the decomposition dynamics of {\it anti-}CH$_3$CHOO are investigated using molecular dynamics simulations on a neural network-based potential energy surface under thermal and mode-selective vibrational excitation. Simulations were performed at internal energies representative of those released during ozonolysis (chemical/thermal preparation, TP) or following vibrational excitation (VibEx) along the CH-stretching mode with two or three quanta, as can be done in laboratory studies. These excitation conditions strongly affect reaction yields and kinetics, with VibEx promoting passage across the initial cyclization barrier. For TP, 35 kcal/mol of internal energy are required to form molecular products, whereas for VibEx, 27 kcal/mol are sufficient. Although TP and VibEx ensembles access largely the same fragmentation pathways with comparable relative yields, the absolute product yields, characteristic timescales, and kinetic behavior differ substantially. title: Network-Wide Freeway Speed Nowcasting and Forecasting from Sparse Fixed Sensors with a Probe-Supervised Graph Convolutional Recurrent Network
abstract: Traffic agencies need current and near-future speeds on every link of their network, but their fixed sensors cover only part of it. We study joint nowcasting and next-hour forecasting of hourly speeds on all 4{,}127 directional freeway links of the Dallas--Fort Worth region from sensors on 643 links (15.6%). Historical probe-vehicle data supervise every link in training; only sensor readings are used at inference. We call this setting probe-supervised sparse sensing. We propose GCRN+, a graph convolutional recurrent network that predicts deviations from a historical speed profile. It combines a parameter-free, direction-aware kernel interpolation of sensor anomalies, used as input features and as an output baseline, with a diffusion-convolutional GRU on the directed road graph, a low-rank adaptive graph and learnable link embeddings. It scales linearly with network size and trains on a CPU. Sensor readings are emulated from probe speeds, which isolates spatio-temporal inference from detector calibration. On four held-out test days, GCRN+ attains an RMSE of 2.21~mph for the current hour and 2.39~mph for the next hour on unsensored links, against 3.23~mph for the historical average.

title: Advancing subseasonal forecasting with machine learning
Retrieving Tropical Cyclone Intensity from Climate Reanalysis using Deep Learning
abstract: Abstract Traditional methods for improving tropical cyclone (TC) intensity from climate model outputs or projections have primarily relied on either dynamical or statistical downscaling. With recent advances in deep learning (DL) techniques, it is of interest to examine how DL can provide an alternative approach for enhancing TC intensity and structure retrieval from climate data. Using a common DL architecture based on convolutional neural networks (CNN) and a set of key environmental features relevant to TCs, we show that TC intensity and size can be effectively retrieved from climate reanalysis data without requiring super-resolution enhancement as in previous studies, even when applied to coarse-resolution climate data. This approach allows for retrieving TC intensity metrics and size that are dynamically constrained by the data, rather than estimating these quantities independently. Our results highlight that TC intensity and size are governed not only by TC internal processes but also by local environments during TC development for which DL models can learn and capture. The performance of our DL model depends on several factors such as season, the stage of TC development, or

title: Variable Masking for Climate Emulation in ACE
abstract: In the recent AI Model Intercomparison Project (AIMIP) benchmark, the ACE2.1-ERA5 emulator was shown to underestimate the true near-surface warming trend both during the training period and the out-of-sample extrapolation period. In this work, we present M-ACE2S (Masked-ACE2S), a modified version of the stochastic ACE2S model, which uses variable masking during training and reduces the reliance of M-ACE2S on any single input channel. We show that M-ACE2S improves long-term near-surface air temperature prediction. We also present a novel data normalization strategy called "global mean removal", which, combined with masking, further improves the near-surface temperature forecasts. We show that M-ACE2S outperforms the ACE2S baseline on in-sample data for ERA5 while improving training stability and generalizability of near-surface temperature to unseen forcing when paired with global mean removal.

title: Improved Precipitation Variability in the Community Atmosphere Model through Implementation of a Neural-Network Deep Convection Scheme
abstract: Conventional deep convection schemes remain a primary source of uncertainty in global climate models, yet replacing them with data-driven alternatives while maintaining physical consistency and numerical stability is an open challenge. We present a hybrid configuration of the Community Atmosphere Model version 6 (CAM6), in which a fully connected deep neural network replaces the Zhang-McFarlane deep convection scheme (ZM), while radiation, turbulence, and other cloud processes are left unchanged. The network is trained on output from a storm-resolving global model - the global System for Atmospheric Modeling (gSAM) - using a coarse-graining approach to derive subgrid-scale convective fluxes and tendencies. This data-driven parameterization is ported to CAM6 and found to run stably for more than a decade while conserving energy and moisture. It produces a broadly realistic climatology without retuning the remaining parameterizations. Relative to the default Zhang-McFarlane scheme, the neural network parameterization substantially improves some long-standing model deficiencies. title: PrecipCorrDiff: A Deep Learning Framework for Generating 0.0625$^\circ$ High-Resolution IMD Gridded Precipitation Data
abstract: High-resolution precipitation datasets are essential for weather forecasting, hydrological modeling, and climate risk assessment, yet observation-based gridded products often lack the spatial detail required for regional applications. Here we present PrecipCorrDiff, a diffusion-based downscaling framework built by modifying the original corrector diffusion based archetecture that incorporates a customized loss function and a multi-scale residual generation strategy to improve the precipitation especially the representation of extremes. PrecipCorrDiff generates 0.0625° resolution India Meteorological Department (IMD) precipitation fields from 0.25° gridded data while preserving precipitation statistics and reconstructing fine-scale spatial variability. Validation against independent IMD station observations, comparing the proposed framework with the SRGAN-based model and the original CorrDiff model, indicates that the proposed framework substantially improves the representation of spatial precipitation patterns, rainfall intensity distributions, and extreme rainfall events, while eliminating the systematic negative bias present in the previously developed SRGAN-based model. title: Generative modelling for multivariate spatio-temporal downscaling of monthly climate fields
abstract: Inferring climate fields at higher spatio-temporal resolutions from coarse representations is essential for accessing socioeconomic and environmental impacts. The downscaling of modelled climate fields faces a trade-off between data storage constraints, simulation efficiency, and resolution requirements. While many methods for spatial downscaling have been proposed, joint spatio-temporal downscaling has received comparable little attention. When deriving, for example, daily fields from climate datasets that are available only as monthly averages at coarser spatial resolution, it is highly challenging to faithfully reproduce extreme event statistics and spatiotemporal consistency. To address this task, we introduce a generative machine learning approach, using a diffusion model to jointly downscale monthly temperature and precipitation fields into temporally consistent daily fields at higher spatial resolution. We demonstrate that our approach can generate high-dimensional multivariate climate fields at daily temporal and 0.25° spatial resolution from monthly input fields at 1° spatial resolution, exhibiting coherent temporal dynamics and physically plausible spatial structures. title: Unmasking Compensating Errors in Numerical Weather Models: A Process-Additive Neural Network Approach
abstract: This work introduces a Process Additive Neural Network (PANN) framework to disentangle compensating biases in atmospheric models, where errors in different physical processes can offset each other and obscure their origins. Using a single-column model, each PANN branch represents the tendency error associated with a separate physical process, and the summed branch outputs approximate the total error relative to a reference tendency. Once trained successfully, the branch outputs are expected to provide process-level error attributions and, when averaged, estimates of process-level bias. Initial experiments focus on cloud-related processes in OpenIFS SCM case studies, where cloud and convection tendencies are strongly coupled and compensation is difficult to diagnose using standard approaches. The aim is not to replace human interpretation of physical processes, but to extend it to regimes where model complexity, process interaction, and compensating errors make direct diagnosis difficult. By providing a physically structured form of machine-learning interpretability, PANN can help connect complex model behaviour with process-level explanations. This work supports both improved under

title: Forecast lead time and the timing of crew deployment for weather-driven power outages using AI weather models
abstract: Utilities request mutual aid crews to restore power after severe storms, and requesting early secures more crews but relies on less accurate forecasts. We examined how forecast lead time affects the value of outage predictions for crew deployment, using operational forecasts from two AI weather models, GraphCast and FourCastNet, to predict outage occurrence for counties across the contiguous United States 24 to 120 hours ahead. Forecasts were evaluated by the share of outage burden captured by the counties where crews would be staged. Captured burden declined with lead time: the loss between three and five days was significant in all analyses, whereas the loss within three days was significant only for outages that had not yet started. Early deployment with all requested crews outperformed late deployment with fewer, and we report the availability ratio at which the two break even. Antecedent land surface predictors computed at forecast valid time include weather from the forecast period, which inflates their skill by 42 to 53% and reverses their apparent advantage over forecast meteorology at long lead times. Computed correctly, they improved occurrence skill by 17.5% at 24 hours

title: Collaborative Neural Networks significantly Improve Global Aerosol Retrievals From Multi-Angle Polarimeters
abstract: We present the RemoTAP-Hybrid algorithm for global aerosol products retrieved from Multi-Angle Polarimeters (MAP), and apply it to one-year aerosol retrievals from the SPEXone MAP instrument. For the first time, Multiple Collaborated Neural Networks (MCNN) are used to perform global aerosol MAP retrievals over land and ocean. The combined use of MCNN with a full physics inversion in RemoTAP-Hybrid, significantly improves accuracy and computational speed of SPEXone aerosol retrievals. We validate the retrieved Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD), Angstrom Exponent (AE), Single Scattering Albedo (SSA), Absorption AOD (AAOD), Fine mode AOD (FAOD), Coarse mode AOD (CAOD), and fine mode effective radius (reff_fine) with AERONET data. The validation suggests that aerosol retrievals can be further improved when extending the aerosol description to include a fine non-spherical mode. For AOD, the Root-Mean-Square Error (RMSE) is 0.051 (0.037) over land (ocean), while 78.3% (80.8%) of the retrievals are within the requirement formulated by the Global Climate Observing System (GCOS). title: Establishing baseline model performances for optical turbulence forecasting
abstract: Accurate forecasting of optical turbulence (OT) is useful to optimise telescope scheduling and maximising observing efficiency, as the performance of adaptive optics systems strongly depends on turbulence conditions. While various numerical weather prediction and machine learning models are developed to predict these complex turbulence properties, properly evaluating their added value requires well-defined baseline reference models. This study establishes baseline performance thresholds for key astroclimatic parameters using two distinct models: one forecasting the parameter average over a specific timescale, and the other forecasting the temporal evolution over the same specific timescale. We apply these frameworks to extensive, multi-year datasets from the sites of the Very Large Telescope (VLT) and the Large Binocular Telescope (LBT) and discuss the possibility of extrapolating reference values of forecast performances for other sites based on their optical turbulence statistical characteristics. title: Extreme events and statistics in an AI emulator of a global storm-resolving model
abstract: We present HiRO-ACEv2 (High Resolution Output Ai2 Climate Emulator), a two-stage framework for AI emulation of the 3~km resolution X-SHiELD global storm-resolving model (GSRM), and highlight its ability to generate large ensembles of data for studying the characteristics of tropical cyclones and extreme events in high-resolution simulations at an inference computational cost over 300 times lower than that of traditional numerical GSRMs. HiRO-ACEv2 expands upon the precipitation-only HiRO-ACEv1 model to generate coherent precipitation, 10~m winds, and sea level pressure outputs, enabling a broader range of events to be simulated at high-resolution. Fine-resolution predictions are generated by running an autoregressive emulator of coarsened X-SHiELD at 100 km, whose multivariate outputs are regionally downscaled to 3~km resolution via a separately trained diffusion model. Particular importance is placed on capturing the statistics of extreme events during the diffusion downscaling step. title: Accounting for model error in ensemble variational data assimilation through learned generative dynamics
abstract: Many approaches have recently been proposed to combine data assimilation with machine learning for improved forecasts with geophysical models. Here, we focus on combining advanced sequential data assimilation schemes with a generative forecasting model which accounts for complex model errors. This generative model provides a stochastic approximation of the conditional distribution of the successor state given the current state. The proposed variational formulation is a novel one-step weak-constraint 4D-Var scheme in which a learned conditional stochastic forecast replaces the prescribed additive Gaussian model error representation. We derive and implement this formulation as an ensemble variational algorithm, the generative iterative ensemble Kalman filter (IEnKF-G), which generalises the iterative ensemble Kalman filter with additive Gaussian model error (IEnKF-Q). We extend the method to a smoother with an assimilation window spanning multiple time steps and propose a simplified variant. title: Identifying Arctic states vulnerable to rapid ice loss with a convolutional neural network
abstract: This work investigates the incidence of rapid ice-loss events in the Arctic, in which a substantial fraction of September sea-ice is lost in only a few years. Such events are seen to occur in climate model simulations forced with increasing greenhouse gas concentrations, but not as yet in the relatively short observational record. We train a convolutional neural network (CNN) using six large climate model ensembles to diagnose vulnerability to rapid ice-loss events. The trained model is shown to separate higher and lower risk states in out-of-sample climate models via a leave-one-out cross-validation. The model emphasises the role of persistently thin sea-ice, remaining sea-ice extent and sustained high upper ocean heat content as predictors of rapid ice-loss. The CNN is applied to observational data over the satelite-era showing a signal for rapid ice-loss prior to a drop around 2007 and an increasing risk from around 2015 to present. Such rapid-ice loss events would likely have dramatic consequences for Arctic ecosystems, coastal communities and global shipping.

title: Super-resolution as Spatial Downscaling: Coherence, Structure and Task Utility in Earth Observation
abstract: Learned satellite super-resolution is commonly assessed by pixel fidelity and potential downlink savings, but these criteria do not establish whether the reconstructed field preserves spatial structure or supports reliable downstream analysis. We treat single-image super-resolution as a spatial downscaling problem and evaluate four lightweight networks, including our compact 0.36 million-parameter model, against interpolation using pixel metrics, directional variograms, spectral band correlation, codispersion and observation coherence. On 735 satellite tiles from 190 scenes, the networks differ by at most 0.03dB and outperform bicubic interpolation by $1.39-1.42$dB at $\times 2$. They recover about 30% of the spectral power above the observation's Nyquist frequency and, at $\times 4$, produce more isotropic fields than the reference (range anisotropy 0.59 against 0.49). Energy-based metrics can favour invented detail. Enforcing coherence reaches the quantisation limit, yet at least 99.7% of the remaining error lies in the observation operator's null space, which coherence cannot constrain. title: Statistical Downscaling of Daily Precipitation from ERA5 Atmospheric Fields to IMERG over West Africa
abstract: Global reanalyses are too coarse to resolve the convective systems that produce most West African monsoon rainfall. In this work, we use U-Net based architectures to downscale daily ERA5 fields (0.25°) to IMERG V07 satellite precipitation (0.1°) over West Africa for the June to October seasons of 2000 to 2024, using geopotential, temperature, humidity and wind at three pressure levels together with elevation and land fraction. Adding ERA5 precipitation as input slightly improves performance for this particular challenging region. We find that all the deterministic networks investigated for this work are too dry and lose almost all observed variance below a few hundred kilometers, which motivated our use of a GAN-based alternative. We also investigated permutation importance for the U-Net that ranks 500 hPa specific humidity first, consistent with the sensitivity of deep convection to mid-tropospheric moisture.

title: AeroChem: Closed-loop Physics-Informed State Space Modeling for Long-term Chemically-Reactive Air Quality Forecasting--Extended Version
abstract: Accurate long-term air quality forecasting is challenging due to long-range transport, meteorological variability, and nonlinear chemical reactions underlying secondary pollutant formation. Purely data-driven models often suffer from long-horizon drift and lack physical consistency, while existing physics-informed approaches commonly follow open-loop designs that fuse neural and physical components only at the output level. We propose AeroChem, a closed-loop physics-informed state space framework for chemically reactive air quality forecasting. AeroChem adopts a two-branch co-correction design: a UDE-based process branch provides a structured but imperfect physical prior, while a Mamba-based virtual measurement branch captures long-range temporal context and produces probabilistic virtual observations. Neural Kalman Fusion couples the two branches by correcting the latent physical state at each forecasting step and feeding the posterior state back into the simulator, reducing long-horizon drift. title: Sensitivity Fidelity Reveals Physical Dependencies Beyond Forecast Accuracy in Deep-Learning Earth-System Models
abstract: Deep-learning models increasingly rival numerical simulation in Earth-system forecasting, yet forecast error alone cannot determine whether their learned input-output dependencies are physically consistent. Here we introduce sensitivity fidelity as an additional criterion: alongside prediction error, model responses to input perturbations should be examined against a trusted reference or established physical knowledge. In an idealized Rayleigh-Bénard convection benchmark, four surrogate architectures achieved low forecast errors yet encoded markedly different sensitivities. Quantitative comparison with a matched adjoint distinguished the models far more sharply than forecast accuracy and showed that predictive skill and sensitivity fidelity need not coincide, while finite-perturbation experiments further linked these differences to the propagation of initial-condition uncertainty. We then applied this strategy to El Niño-Southern Oscillation prediction, where no adjoint reference exists and learned sensitivities showed event-wise robustness, validity under finite perturbations, and consistency with established precursors. title: Probabilistic Forecasting of Wildfire Size Using Conditional Flow Matching
abstract: In this work we present a probabilistic model for predicting the temporal evolution of wildfire size using conditional generative algorithms, namely flow matching. Rather than predicting spatially resolved fire progression, the proposed model forecasts a time series of fire acreage, substantially reducing computational cost and enabling efficient integration with downstream applications such as early warning systems and risk assessment tools. Given estimates of the fire size at the current and previous forecasting steps, alongside spatially averaged weather conditions, terrain characteristics, and fuel composition, the model predicts the change in fire area over a 3-hour interval. Training data are drawn from 140 coupled atmosphere-wildfire simulations generated using WRF-SFIRE, paired with weather data from the North American Mesoscale (NAM) model. Sensitivity analysis demonstrates that the model captures physically-consistent responses to variations in wind speed, temperature, and relative humidity. Model performance is evaluated against reference solutions from WRF-SFIRE. For single-step predictions, the model achieves a symmetric mean absolute percentage error (sMAPE) of 0.39 r

title: OceanFlow: Coherent Flow Matching for Probabilistic Ocean Modeling
abstract: Probabilistic ocean modeling is essential for risk-aware marine operations, climate analysis, and scientific decision-making, where downstream decisions depend on the conditional distribution of future ocean states rather than a single deterministic trajectory. Recent data-driven ocean models have made deterministic global ocean modeling increasingly accurate and efficient, but probabilistic ocean modeling remains underdeveloped. Specifically, perturbation-driven ensembles can create spread without explicitly optimizing the joint distribution of their members, often yielding poor calibration and physical inconsistency. To address these issues, we propose OceanFlow, a coherent flow matching framework for probabilistic global ocean modeling. OceanFlow first establishes a sharp, stable mean anchor for the conditional ensemble. Flow matching then learns a coherent state-conditioned pathwise law that jointly reshapes the residual distribution around this anchor at each transition, preserving the predictive center while refining state-dependent uncertainty. title: Deep-learning climate emulator ACE2 reveals a global decrease in 15th-century tropical cyclone frequency under El Niño-like sea surface temperatures
Learning native eddy-resolving ocean dynamics outperforms coarse emulation and downscaling
abstract: Eddy-resolving ocean simulations are essential for representing mesoscale dynamics that regulate ocean circulation, energy transport, and climate variability. However, they are costly to generate, store, and share. Artificial intelligence (AI) may help, but it remains unclear whether high-resolution ocean fields can be faithfully represented by evolving ocean states at coarse resolution followed by spatial downscaling, or whether dynamical evolution needs to be learned directly from native high-resolution simulations. We show that directly learning dynamical evolution on a 0.1$^\circ$ grid provides a more faithful representation of mesoscale variability than evolving ocean states on a 1$^\circ$ grid followed by downscaling reconstruction. We developed a full-depth 1$^\circ$ emulator and a native 0.1$^\circ$ sea surface temperature (SST) emulator, both of which remained stable over long-term free-running simulations without significant drift, providing reliable baselines for this comparison. title: WeatherBridge: Forecast-Aware Multi-Source Input Adaptation for Pretrained Weather Forecasting Models
abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting models are commonly trained on ERA5, yet operational deployment must use timely initial states from physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems whose distributions differ substantially from ERA5. Direct initialization with these states can degrade autoregressive forecasts, motivating input adaptation that keeps the pretrained forecasting model unchanged. Here, we introduce WeatherBridge, a unified, source-conditioned adapter that maps heterogeneous operational NWP initial states to ERA5 reference states without updating the pretrained forecasting model. WeatherBridge predicts the structured residual corrections with a Swin-UNet and injects source embeddings across multiple spatial scales, allowing the model to capture shared atmospheric structure and source-specific discrepancies. Its training objective combines latitude-weighted ERA5 reconstruction with One-step Rollout Alignment (ORA), which backpropagates one-step forecast error through a frozen FuXi model to optimize the adapted states for both initial state fidelity and downstream forecast compatibility. title: Diffusion Precipitation Generation with Medium-range Weather Forecasting
abstract: Accurate daily precipitation forecasts are important for weather-sensitive decisions. Although recent Weather Foundation Models (WFMs) have achieved significant progress, they are trained on reanalysis data, which exhibit regional and intensity-dependent biases. Since retraining WFMs on observation-based targets is costly, we study Dynamics-Precipitation Decoupling, a plug-and-play framework that uses a separately trained generator to map non-precipitation forecasts from a frozen weather model to observation-aligned daily precipitation. Its key challenges are to capture heterogeneous rainfall distributions and align daily accumulations with atmospheric signals that evolve across space and time. To address them, we train a diffusion generator conditional on atmospheric states and satellite-gauge estimates of precipitation. A multi-scale recurrent encoder summarizes atmospheric evolution, while cross-attention aligns atmospheric and precipitation features during denoising. title: legoESM: a modular, differentiable, multiscale, AI-ready Earth system model built with AI agents
abstract: Earth system models (ESMs) have grown tremendously in realism, yet key uncertainties persist in the climate response to greenhouse-gas forcing, particularly due to cloud radiative feedbacks. In addition, their software architecture was not designed for accelerator hardware or modern artificial intelligence (AI). Here we present legoESM, a composable, differentiable, multiscale ESM written in JAX. It builds on decades of community-developed parameterizations and numerical methods, recast in a unified framework by AI coding agents under a human-specified scientific contract and verified through benchmarking. Dynamical cores, physics schemes, grids, complexity levels and components are swappable like building blocks, and can use conventional physics or machine-learned emulators. A single code base spans metre-scale large-eddy simulation to global simulations and weather to climate. End-to-end differentiability enables gradient-based calibration, variational data assimilation and online training. legoESM modular architecture enables systematic evaluation of diverse model variants to explore structural uncertainty and test hypotheses. legoESM produces realistic simulations across scales

title: A Physics-Constrained Implicit Profile Network for Continuous Reconstruction of Tropical Cyclone Near-Surface Wind Profiles
abstract: Near the ocean surface, tropical cyclone winds change rapidly with height, but direct measurements are limited because aircraft dropsondes provide only sparse and irregular observations. Continuous wind profiles are important for understanding hurricane boundary-layer processes, improving storm-surge prediction, supporting offshore engineering, and assessing coastal hazards. In this study, we developed an artificial intelligence model that combines machine learning with physical principles to reconstruct continuous wind profiles from sparse observations. The model is designed to preserve the observed surface winds while generating realistic changes in wind speed and direction with height. Tests using more than two decades of NOAA hurricane observations show that the method accurately reproduces the vertical structure of tropical cyclone winds over a wide range of storm intensities. The framework can also extend satellite-derived surface wind measurements into three-dimensional near-surface wind fields, providing new opportunities for hurricane research, operational forecasting, and engineering applications.

title: A Graph Neural Network for Global Daily Fire Radiative Power Prediction at Medium-Range Lead Times
abstract: Skillful prediction of biomass-burning activity several days in advance is important for air-quality forecasting and aerosol prediction. Two operational constraints motivate this work. First, the GBBEPx satellite fire radiative power (FRP) product used to initialize NOAA's GEFS-Aerosols is available with about a 1.5-day latency, so each forecast cycle relies on the most recently available, but already outdated, fire observations. Second, these fire inputs are then held fixed throughout the subsequent 5-day operational forecast, or 7 days in the GSL experimental system, effectively assuming no evolution in fire activity. We develop a data-driven model that predicts global FRP one to seven days ahead from the most recent available observations. The model adapts a spatiotemporal graph neural network using reanalysis meteorology, land-cover and vegetation information, recent fire history, and GBBEPx FRP as the training target. It is trained on 2020-2022 data and evaluated for 2023-2024. The model reproduces the global seasonal cycle and substantially outperforms persistence.
